text: A load balancer sits in front of a group of backend servers and spreads incoming traffic across them instead of sending every request to one single machine. That solves two different problems at once: availability, since if one instance crashes or is being patched the rest keep serving requests without users ever noticing, and scale, since you add more modestly sized instances behind it as demand grows instead of trying to build one giant server that can handle everything alone.

A Layer 4 load balancer works at the transport layer — it looks only at IP addresses and port numbers and forwards packets based on that, without inspecting what's actually inside the request. It doesn't know or care if traffic is an API call for slash login or slash images, it just sees TCP traffic headed for a port and routes it. That makes Layer 4 load balancing very fast and low-overhead. AWS's Network Load Balancer is a real example, built for raw throughput and extremely low latency.

A Layer 7 load balancer, by contrast, actually reads the HTTP request — the URL path, headers, cookies — and can make smarter routing decisions based on content, not just IP and port. That's what lets it send slash api requests to one backend pool and slash images requests to a completely different one, all from a single load balancer sitting in front of several backend services. AWS's Application Load Balancer is the real example, and it can route by URL path exactly like that.

Both layers rely on health checks — the load balancer periodically pings each backend instance, often with a simple HTTP request to a health endpoint, to confirm it's actually responding correctly. If an instance fails enough consecutive checks, the load balancer marks it unhealthy and stops routing traffic to it until it starts passing checks again. That's the real mechanism behind the availability benefit from earlier: the load balancer isn't guessing which instance is broken, it's continuously verifying.
